name: Liability When Agents Interact
title: Liability When Agents Interact
answer: Liability when agents interact covers the legal questions that arise when two or more autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents exchange instructions, negotiate, transact, or act on shared systems and a loss, breach, or injury follows. It sits within emerging legal frameworks and draws on tort, contract, product liability, agency, and data protection law. The central difficulty is that harm may emerge from a sequence of interactions rather than a single act, so causation and fault are hard to assign to one developer, deployer, operator, or user. The site's tracker of 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, shows that disputes over AI conduct already reach court.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What this work runs on is both technical and legal. On the technical side, agents interact through APIs, message queues, identity and access systems, orchestration platforms, and shared environments, and each of these leaves or fails to leave records. On the legal side, the interaction runs on the contracts, terms of service, licenses, indemnities, insurance policies, and permissioning rules that connect the parties. Provenance depends on whether logs, model versions, prompts, and decision traces are retained well enough to reconstruct who did what.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of assigning liability is done by reconstructing the interaction from logs, prompts, model outputs, configuration files, and human oversight records, then mapping that sequence onto existing legal duties. Practitioners compare the facts to doctrines such as negligence, strict product liability, breach of contract, and respondeat superior, and they test whether an agent's action can be attributed to a person or firm. The site's 29 AI case law precedents offer starting points for analogy, even where the underlying technology differs. Experts may also run controlled replays or red team exercises to see whether an interaction was foreseeable or preventable.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance are the core governance concerns when agents interact. Rights questions include who owns outputs, who may use data exchanged between agents, and what license terms apply to each step. Risk is allocated through contracts, indemnities, insurance, and regulatory duties, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages and 6979 state AI bills reflect how quickly those duties are being proposed. Provenance requires records of data lineage, model identity, permissions, and decision history, because without them a dispute can stall on basic questions of what happened.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon points toward more agent-to-agent commerce, more standard interaction protocols, and more disputes over allocation of loss. As the site's current count shows, 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents indicate that courts are still building the vocabulary for these cases. Legislatures and regulators are likely to add clarity through state AI bills and compliance guidance, though the pace and shape remain uncertain. Insurance markets and contract drafting practices will probably adapt as parties seek predictable ways to price and assign the risk of interacting agents.
